Introduction

For most people, what we believe about God is initially determined by the family or culture in which
we grow up. If you have parents who are Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, Jewish, or parents
of any other religion, or if you grow up in a culture which predominantly believes in one of those religions, then your initial belief about God is likely to be similar to your parents or to that culture.
The reverse is also true, and increasingly in this secular world, if you grow up with atheist or agnostic
parents, or within an atheistic or agnostic culture, you are likely to grow up to be an atheist or agnostic.
This book is not about any individual religion, but it is concerned with the Jewish, Christian and Islamic religions that are often grouped together under the term of ‘monotheistic’ or belief in a single
God.
It is not a book which concerns itself with the teaching of any one of those individual belief system,
but rather a book that transcends religious and denominational differences to concentrate upon the attributes of the God in which all three of those religions believe.
It is a book about the scientific evidence for God, and for the scientific evidence for the attributes of
God, rather than a book about any specific religion.
Nothing in this book proves there is a God, or that there is not a God, but its main premise is that
God and science are not incompatible. On the contrary, cutting-edge science has reached the stage
where it now provides an understanding about God which could only be guessed at previously. God
and science are now complementary rather than contradictory.
Each chapter of the book outlines the science that supports one of God's attributes, and this is followed by a chapter about the philosophical consequences of those attributes and conclusions.
Not everyone will agree with the science, because much of it is new and not yet commonly accepted.
I expect even fewer will agree with my philosophical conclusions, which are sometimes at odds with the
world's major religions, and which may require a paradigm shift or change of perspective.
